chapter.title: Work orders in small pieces: one feature at a time

cards.body:
You wouldn't tell a contractor 'redo the kitchen, the bathroom and the roof' and then leave for a week. You'd say 'kitchen cabinets first', walk in when they're up, open a few doors, and only then hand over the next job.

That's the whole chapter: **one work order at a time**. Picture a clipboard with 6 numbered lines, and a tick beside each one as it gets done and checked.
cards.simpler:
Imagine hiring a builder. You wouldn't say 'fix the kitchen, the bathroom and the roof' and then leave for a week. You'd say 'kitchen cabinets first', come back when they're up, open a few doors, and then hand over the next job.

This chapter is about doing the same with Claude: **one work order at a time**. Picture a clipboard with six numbered lines, and a tick beside each one once it is done and checked.

cards.prompt: Your friend Dev types into Claude Code: 'Build me a recipe app with search, photos, a shopping list, dark mode and sign-in.' Claude works for 4 minutes. The page opens blank. What's the most likely trouble?

options.text: Recipe apps are too hard for Claude; it ran out of ideas.
Five jobs went in at once, so when one broke there's no way to tell which.
Dark mode always breaks pages; he should have asked for light mode.

whyNot.a: That's a size problem, not a skill problem: Claude can build each of those 5 things, just not reliably all in one go.
whyNot.c: That's blaming one feature by guessing: with 5 changes landing together, nobody can know which one broke the page.

cards.reteach: Think of the contractor. If 5 crews work on the house at once and the lights go out, who do you ask? Hand over one job, check it, then the next. Then a problem can only have one cause.

cards.title: Why one job beats five
cards.body:
When Claude builds one feature, it changes a few files for one reason. If the app still works, that feature is fine. If it breaks, **the cause is inside that one change**.

When it builds 5 features at once, it changes many files for 5 reasons. Something breaks, and now you and Claude are both guessing. The fix for one thing often breaks a second thing.

So the loop is short: ask for one job, test it as a user, save it with Git (the commit from chapter 5), then the next job. A saved good version after each step means the worst case is losing 10 minutes, not the afternoon.
cards.simpler:
When Claude builds one feature, it changes a few files for one reason. If something breaks, **the cause is inside that one change**.

Build five at once and many files change for five reasons. Now something breaks, and you both guess. Fixing one thing often breaks another.

So keep the loop short: one job, test it like a user, save it with Git (chapter 5), then the next. Worst case, you lose ten minutes, not the afternoon.

cards.title: Maya's bill splitter
cards.body:
Maya wants an app to split a restaurant bill. Her list: 1. a page with a box for the total. 2. a box for how many people. 3. show each person's share. 4. a tip slider. 5. a 'copy result' button. 6. make it look right on a phone.

Job 3 came back dividing by an empty box, so the page said each friend owed *Infinity*. Because job 3 was **the only thing that had changed**, she described it in one line and Claude fixed it in under a minute. Some friends do try to pay Infinity, but the app shouldn't ask.
cards.simpler:
Maya wants an app to split a bill. Her six jobs: a box for the total, a box for how many people, each person's share, a tip slider, a copy button, and a layout that fits a phone.

Job 3 came back dividing by an empty box, so the page said each friend owed Infinity. Because job 3 was **the only thing that had changed**, she described it in one line and Claude fixed it in under a minute.

cards.prompt: Sam wants a habit tracker. Which first job should he hand to Claude?

options.text: 'Make a habit tracker that saves my habits, shows streaks, sends reminders and syncs to my phone.'
'Show a page with a list of 3 habit names I type in. Nothing else yet.'
'Set up the whole project so everything will be easy to add later.'

whyNot.a: That's the whole house in one work order: 4 features, and if the page comes up blank you can't tell which one did it.
whyNot.c: That's a job you can't test: 'easy to add later' isn't something you can click and watch work, so you never know when it's done.

cards.reteach: A good job is one you can test by using the app for 30 seconds. 'Show a list of habits I type' passes: type 3, see 3. 'Set up everything' can't be checked, so it isn't a job yet.

cards.title: How to cut an idea into jobs
cards.body:
Start with the plainest version that does one useful thing. For a bill splitter, that's a total, a head count and a share. Write that as job 1.

Then add one thing per line until you have 5 to 8 lines. Each line must pass the *30-second test*: you can open the app, do the thing, and see it work in under 30 seconds. If a line fails that test, it's really 2 jobs. Split it.

Keep the list in a file inside your project, called something like todo.md. Then tell Claude: **'Do job 1 only. Stop and tell me when it's ready to test.'** That last sentence is the whole trick.
cards.simpler:
Start with the plainest useful version. For a bill splitter, job 1 is a total, a head count and a share.

Add one line at a time until you have 5 to 8. Each line must pass the 30-second test: open the app, do the thing, see it work, in under 30 seconds. If a line fails, split it in two.

Then tell Claude: **'Do job 1 only. Stop and tell me when it's ready to test.'**

cards.body:
Priya had a clean list of 7 jobs. Job 2 went so well that she got brave and typed 'now do 3, 4 and 5'. Job 4 broke the page, and the fix Claude tried quietly undid job 3. She spent 40 minutes getting back to where job 2 had left her.

The tell is easy to spot: **your request has a comma-separated list of features**, or the word 'and' more than once.
cards.simpler:
Priya had a clean list of seven jobs. Job 2 went so well that she got brave and typed 'now do 3, 4 and 5'. Job 4 broke the page. The fix Claude tried quietly undid job 3. She spent 40 minutes just getting back to where job 2 had left her.

The warning sign is easy to spot: **your request has a list of features separated by commas**, or the word 'and' shows up more than once.

cards.prompt: You finish job 4 of 6 and the app works. What comes right before you type job 5?

options.text: Save a version with Git, so job 4 is safe if job 5 breaks things.
Delete the todo file, since you remember the rest.
Ask Claude to do jobs 5 and 6 together to make up time.

whyNot.b: That's throwing away the clipboard: the list is what keeps your next session on track, and Claude can read it too.
whyNot.c: That's Priya's move: bundling 2 jobs means if one breaks you can't tell which, and the fix may undo the other.

cards.reteach: The loop has 3 beats: ask for one job, test it, save it. Skip the save and the next broken job costs you the last good one too.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Cut the app into 5 to 8 jobs you can each test in 30 seconds, and hand Claude **one at a time**. Test it, save it, then the next: a breakage can only have one cause, and you never lose more than one job's work.
cards.simpler: Cut your app into 5 to 8 jobs. Each one should be something you can test in 30 seconds. Hand them to Claude **one at a time**. Test the result, save it, then move to the next. This way a breakage can only have one cause, and you never lose more than one job's worth of work.

cards.body: Open a blank note. Write your app idea as job 1: the plainest thing that does one useful job. Add lines until you have 5 to 8. Cross out any line that fails the 30-second test and split it in two.
cards.simpler: Open a blank note. Write your app idea as job 1: the plainest thing that does one useful job. Keep adding lines until you have 5 to 8. Now check each line against the 30-second test. Can you open the app, do the thing, and see it work that fast? If a line fails, cross it out and **split it into two smaller jobs**.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now turn an app idea into 5 to 8 small jobs and build them one at a time, with a saved version after each.
